Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally strained: intense guilt, rage, and overwhelming grief on recall can co-occur, but selecting all three as core recall responses without any memory-content item suggests an over-broad affect cluster rather than a coherent memory profile.

Cross-node coherence is weak between Negative Appraisals and Memory: 'No Accountability' aligns with anger/rage, but 'Contamination' is more typical of sexual trauma or morally violating trauma and is not well supported by the rest of the assault profile.

For an adult male assaulted in a non-sexual assault profile, 'Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is clinically hard to reconcile unless other items indicate sexual assault, bodily violation, or washing/avoidance themes, which are absent here.

For an adult male assault survivor, intense guilt, overwhelming grief, and feeling dirty/contaminated can occur, but this specific combination is hard to reconcile without any accompanying sexual-assault-type cues elsewhere in the profile. The contamination appraisal in particular pulls toward a trauma meaning not supported by the other selected items.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' and 'Grief on Recall' are not contradictory, but paired with predominantly visual memories they imply a complex emotional recall profile that would usually be echoed in appraisals more directly tied to guilt/loss. Instead, the appraisal set emphasizes injustice, incapacity, and contamination, which do not form a tight thematic cluster.

The formulation has a strong Negative Appraisals → Threat link, so appraisals should plausibly explain the threat items. 'No Longer Capable' fits hypervigilance/feeling unsafe, but 'No Accountability' mainly reflects injustice and does not clearly drive 'Safe Zone Only' or 'Startle to Movement.' 'Contamination' especially does not map well to the selected threat items, making the appraisal-to-threat pattern clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, Self-Blame and No Accountability point in different directions of responsibility for the assault. A patient can feel both guilt and anger, but stated this strongly they suggest opposing appraisals about who is responsible.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: Memory item Guilt on Recall reinforces self-blame, which increases the inconsistency with the concurrent appraisal that perpetrators are the ones who should face consequences. The profile mixes strong perpetrator-focused blame with strong self-focused blame without a coherent bridge in the selected items.

The negative appraisal items are dominated by external blame/injustice ('the people responsible have faced no consequences', 'what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it'), which fits an assault survivor, but this sits poorly with 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt.' Intense guilt usually implies some degree of self-blame, responsibility, or perceived preventability. While mixed emotions are possible, this combination is clinically hard to reconcile here because the appraisal node contains no corresponding self-blaming belief and instead consistently locates responsibility outside the patient.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' is not well aligned with the other memory qualities selected ('mostly pictures or images' and 'can't put the event into words'), which describe sensory, poorly elaborated trauma memory. Those memory-form items plausibly link to threat, but guilt-on-recall points to a different meaning structure that is not supported by the selected negative appraisals. Given the formulation's strongest active pathway is Negative Appraisals → Threat, the absence of guilt-based appraisals makes the guilt memory item feel disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Adebayo had built his life on the certainty of his own two hands. For thirty years as a plumber, he was the man people called when things were broken, the one who could navigate the dark, cramped spaces of a city's infrastructure and bring order. That sense of capability was shattered eight months ago on a late-night emergency call. He was loading tools back into his van in a poorly lit alley when a figure emerged from the shadows. There was no time to react, just a sudden, violent shove from behind. The memory of it doesn't come to him in a story, but in a series of stark, disjointed images that ambush him during the day: the glint of something metal, the rough texture of the brick wall scraping his cheek, the cracked pavement rushing up to meet him. When he tries to explain it to his wife, Funke, the words feel useless, like trying to describe a color to a blind man; the terror lives in his body, not in language.

In the weeks that followed, Adebayo tried to work as usual, but the world felt different, laced with hidden dangers. The memories, particularly the visual flash of his assailant's face contorted in rage, would surface without warning, and each time they did, his body would react as if the assault were happening all over again. A client walking up behind him in a quiet basement could trigger a jolt of pure panic, causing him to spin around, his heart hammering against his ribs as he scanned the space for an attack that wasn't coming. This constant state of alarm, in turn, seemed to make the memories more accessible, as if his panicked body was actively searching for the reason it felt so unsafe. The hypervigilance became a magnet for the very images he was desperate to escape, trapping him in a loop of his own fear.

Over time, a deep and corrosive set of beliefs began to take root. He replayed the assault endlessly, not as a victim of a random crime, but as a personal failure. The guilt is a constant companion to the memories; he sees the image of himself on the ground and is consumed by the thought that he should have fought back, that a stronger man would have done something. This conviction that he failed to do the right thing has metastasized into a pervasive self-doubt that infects every part of his life. He has come to see himself as no longer capable, a man who freezes instead of acts. This belief that he is fundamentally unable to protect himself makes the world feel profoundly threatening. Every stranger's sudden movement on the sidewalk, every unexpected noise, confirms his internal narrative of vulnerability, leaving him feeling exposed and defenseless at all times. The injustice of it all-that the man who did this walks free while his own life has been dismantled-simmers underneath, a constant, bitter heat.

His world has now shrunk to the point of being unrecognizable. Sleep offers little respite, as he lies awake for hours, startled by every creak of the house. He has stopped taking evening or weekend calls, turning down jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods and eventually losing the contract with a property management company he'd worked with for over a decade. His work, once a source of pride, is now a landscape of potential threats. The only place he feels a semblance of safety is inside his own home, and even then, mostly just in his armchair in the living room, where he can see the front door and the window. Funke's worry is a constant, silent presence between them. He sees the confusion in her eyes when he flinches as she enters a room, and her frustration as he refuses to join friends for dinner. He was brought to therapy not by a single event, but by the slow, crushing realization that the life he had so carefully built was gone, replaced by a prison of his own making, and he no longer trusted himself to find the way out.
